Case · Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation · Product Metrics & Measurement

Lekha Systems: Seventy-One Per Cent

Bengaluru, the night of Sunday 8 March 2026. A board meeting at ten the next morning, a term sheet with an expiry date, and a number that has gone up for three quarters which the vice-president of product no longer believes.

1. Sunday night, Indiranagar

Kavya Srinivasan had been at the dining table since half past eight, and by a quarter past eleven the table held four things: a printed board deck with the pages out of order, her laptop showing a query she had run six times, a cold cup of filter coffee, and a single sheet of A4 on which she had written two numbers, 71% and 52%, and drawn a box around neither.

The board of Lekha Systems met at ten the following morning in the company's office off 100 Feet Road. Page nine of the deck, which Kavya had written, reported that 71% of new customers reached what Lekha called the automation threshold within sixty days of go-live, up from 44% three quarters earlier. It was the product organisation's flagship number. It was the number Anirudh Varma, the chief executive, had shown to a Singapore growth fund in January, and it sat in a published customer case study that Lekha's American sales head cited in roughly two-fifths of his open pipeline.

On Wednesday, 4 March, a product manager on the payables team had mentioned in passing, in a corridor, that the automation threshold had probably been helped by the auto-approve rule. Kavya had spent Thursday and Friday finding out what that meant. Recomputed with sub-₹25,000 invoices excluded from the touchless count, the same metric for the same quarter was 52%. Recomputed further, on the subset of customers running on the main product rather than the forked enterprise build, it was 49%, and for the forked build it could not be computed at all in a way that was comparable, because the fork's event schema had never been aligned.

None of this, by itself, would have kept her at the table. What kept her there was Tanya Oberoi's message from Toronto, timestamped 19:42 IST on Saturday, which contained a two-line query result and no commentary: in the mid-market book, accounts that reached the automation threshold inside sixty days had churned at a higher rate over the following year than accounts that had not. Fifteen points higher.

2. Company history, and the decision that still constrains it

Lekha Systems was founded in Bengaluru in 2019 by Anirudh Varma and Kavya Srinivasan, both formerly of a large Indian systems-integration firm, to solve a narrow and tedious problem: Indian mid-market companies received purchase invoices in eleven formats and reconciled them by hand. Lekha's first product read an invoice, matched it to a purchase order and a goods-receipt note, flagged the exceptions and pushed the clean ones into whatever ledger the company already ran — Tally, most often, or SAP at the upper end.

The timing was fortunate. The staged extension of India's GST e-invoicing mandate down the turnover thresholds between 2020 and 2023 turned reconciliation from a back-office chore into a compliance obligation with penalties attached, and Lekha's ability to reconcile the government's invoice registration portal data against a company's own books became the reason customers bought. By FY26 the company had 1,340 paying customers and annualised revenue of ₹214 crore, competing against Zoho's finance suite on price and breadth, against Clear on compliance depth, against Razorpay's payables product on the payment leg, and, most stubbornly, against the inertia of Tally plus two clerks.

The decision that still constrained everything was made in November 2022. Al Mirzam Holdings, a Dubai building-materials and retail group with nine subsidiaries and Indian sourcing operations in Morbi and Rajkot, agreed to a three-year contract worth ₹31 crore — at the time, a fifth of Lekha's revenue — on the condition that Lekha build multi-entity consolidation, Arabic-language invoice capture and a custom approval matrix, and commit to service levels that the standard product did not offer. Rajat Bhandari, then Lekha's fourth engineer and now head of engineering in Pune, argued that the work be done in the main codebase behind feature flags. He was overruled on schedule grounds. A fork was created, called Lekha Enterprise internally and, in the deck, "the enterprise edition".

Three and a half years later the fork served forty-one accounts producing ₹79 crore of revenue, consumed roughly 30% of engineering capacity, and — the detail that mattered on the night of 8 March — emitted a different set of product events than the main build. Nobody had decided that Lekha would be unable to measure its two halves the same way. It was a consequence.

3. The industry

The Indian mid-market finance-automation market in early 2026 had three uncomfortable features. First, it was compressing on price. Zoho's bundled finance suite priced per-user at a level Lekha could not match, and Tally's installed base remained the true competitor: most lost deals at Lekha were lost not to another vendor but to a decision to do nothing. Second, it was becoming a compliance market rather than a productivity market, which shifted the buying centre from the finance controller to the chief financial officer and lengthened cycles. Third, the payment leg was consolidating: Razorpay and PhonePe's business products, and the banks' own corporate portals, were absorbing payouts, which meant Lekha's value had to sit in the reconciliation and exception layer or nowhere.

Regulation bore on the product in two directions at once. The e-invoicing mandate created demand. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, whose operational requirements Lekha's counsel had begun applying from mid-2025, removed instrumentation: vendor contact records inside customer invoices were personal data, and the consent re-architecture that went live on 15 January 2026 stopped Lekha collecting supplier-level portal activity in the form it previously had. Tanya Oberoi's best leading indicator of renewal — weekly active suppliers on the vendor portal — therefore had a discontinuity in the middle of the exact period the board would be asked to interpret.

Lekha's global exposure ran along two lines. Al Mirzam in Dubai was its largest account and its most demanding, and Grace Chan, the customer-success lead in Singapore, carried it. Nikhil Iyengar, hired in New Jersey in mid-2025, was building a United States book aimed at mid-market distributors, where Lekha's pitch was not compliance but a hard productivity claim: "seventy-one per cent of our customers reach automation within sixty days." Salary arithmetic made the American experiment fragile — Nikhil's fully loaded cost was roughly what four senior engineers in Pune cost — and it made the touchless claim load-bearing in a way that no one in Bengaluru had fully registered.

4. The situation, in sequence

In April 2025, following a strategy offsite, Lekha adopted what it called an input-led operating model. The reasoning was sound and was Kavya's. Net revenue retention, the number the board tracked, could be read only after a renewal cycle, which for Lekha's annual contracts meant twelve months; no product team could be held to it. So the product organisation adopted Activation-60: the share of new customers reaching the automation threshold — 70% of invoices processed without human touch in a calendar month — within sixty days of go-live. It was controllable, readable in eight weeks, and plausibly causal. It went on page nine.

Through FY26 it performed. The onboarding team shortened the master-data import, the capture team improved the purchase-order matching model, and a self-serve rules builder shipped in July. Activation-60 moved from 44% to 58% to 66% to 71%.

In August 2025, Jonas Keller's design team in Berlin shipped an auto-approve rule, requested by nineteen customers, which allowed a company to approve invoices below a configurable threshold without review. The default threshold was ₹25,000. It was popular; by January 2026, 61% of mid-market customers had it enabled. Nobody connected it to Activation-60, because the two things lived in different teams' sprint reviews. Auto-approved invoices are, definitionally, processed without human touch.

In November 2025, Meghna Rao, the chief financial officer, raised for the first time that the net-revenue-retention figure used in the board deck differed from the one in her own model. The deck's 108% included the amortised module fees from the Al Mirzam contract; her 103% did not. The two of them agreed to reconcile it "after the audit", and did not.

In January 2026, the DPDP consent re-architecture broke the vendor-portal series. In the same month Anirudh took a term sheet conversation to an advanced stage with the Singapore fund, using the deck's numbers.

On 4 March the corridor conversation happened. On 6 March Tanya, working late in Toronto on the mid-market churn cut Kavya had requested, produced Exhibit 4 and wrote a single line in the file: "I don't think this is what we assumed."

5. The people

Anirudh Varma, chief executive, Bengaluru. Position: the board meeting is a checkpoint on a Series C, not a research seminar; restating three quarters of the flagship metric two weeks before a term sheet decision would be reckless. Incentive: the round, and a valuation anchored to a growth narrative. Not saying: he has already shared the 71% and the 108% with two funds in writing, and he does not know whether that constitutes a representation he would have to correct.

Kavya Srinivasan, vice-president of product, Bengaluru. Position: unformed, which is the problem. Incentive: her credibility is the metric's credibility; she chose it. Not saying: she suspected in September that auto-approve might affect the touchless count and noted it in a document nobody read, including, after a while, her.

Meghna Rao, chief financial officer, Bengaluru. Position: net revenue retention must be defined once, in writing, and the 103% cut is the defensible one. Incentive: an auditor's questions land on her desk, not on product's. Not saying: her own variable pay is tied to reported annualised revenue growth, which the module-fee treatment flatters, so her preferred retention definition and her preferred revenue definition are not consistent with each other.

Rajat Bhandari, head of engineering, Pune, 84 engineers across Pune and Bengaluru. Position: none of this is fixable while the fork exists; unify the codebase and the event schema in FY27. Incentive: engineering leverage, and the 30% of his capacity currently spent on forty-one accounts. Not saying: two of his four senior engineers on the fork have told him privately they will leave if they are still on it in July, and he has begun moving one of them without telling Grace.

Nikhil Iyengar, sales head, New Jersey. Position: do not touch the published claim; the United States pipeline for FY27 is ₹4.6 crore of new revenue and 40% of it cites the case study. Incentive: quota and the survival of the American experiment. Not saying: a mid-market distributor in Ohio has already asked, through its procurement function, for the definition behind the 71% and for confirmation that it is independently verifiable.

Grace Chan, customer-success lead, Singapore, covering APAC and the Gulf. Position: exempt the enterprise segment from product metrics entirely; forty-one accounts are managed by relationship, not by dashboard. Incentive: retention of a book that includes Al Mirzam. Not saying: she has granted Al Mirzam informal concessions on exception-resolution turnaround that appear in no contract and in no metric, and which Rajat's engineers have been quietly absorbing.

Tanya Oberoi, data scientist, Toronto. Position: restate the metric, and validate any replacement before it goes on a slide. Incentive: analytical integrity; she is also the person who would have to build the replacement. Not saying: her vendor-portal renewal model was fitted on 900 accounts of which 780 sit in one segment and one price band, and she is not confident it generalises — a caveat present in her notebook and absent from the summary she circulated in December.

Jonas Keller, design lead, Berlin. Position: raise the auto-approve threshold to ₹50,000; the research shows customers want it and the feature is the most-liked thing Lekha shipped in 2025. Incentive: shipped design outcomes and a usage story. Not saying: his own usability sessions found that seven of twelve finance users could not state what "touchless" meant, and two believed it meant Lekha had verified the invoice.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1. Net revenue retention, two ways. Series A is the figure used in board decks since Q1 FY25 and includes amortised custom-module fees from the Al Mirzam contract. Series B is the finance model's figure, which excludes them. Neither has been audited. The definitions were never reconciled; both are computed on a trailing twelve-month basis over accounts live at the start of the window.
QuarterNRR, series A (deck)NRR, series B (finance)Gross churn, mid-marketGross churn, enterprise
Q1 FY25104%101%9.1%2.4%
Q2 FY25106%102%9.4%0.0%
Q3 FY25107%103%10.2%2.4%
Q4 FY25109%105%10.6%0.0%
Q1 FY26108%104%12.8%2.4%
Q2 FY26108%103%14.1%4.9%
Q3 FY26108%103%15.6%2.4%

Enterprise gross churn is computed on 41 accounts, so a single loss moves it 2.4 points. Q2 FY26 reflects two losses.

Exhibit 1 is the exhibit Anirudh reads and the exhibit Meghna reads, and they are not the same exhibit. Series A is flat at 108% and supports the story that Lekha's retention is world-class for an Indian mid-market vendor. Series B is flat at 103% and supports nothing in particular. Both series conceal the same thing, which is in the third column: mid-market gross churn has risen by six and a half points in eight quarters while net retention held, because expansion inside the surviving accounts and the enterprise book covered the loss.

Exhibit 2. Activation-60, as reported and as recomputed. The "as reported" column is what appears on page nine. The consolidated figure blends two product builds whose event schemas differ; the main-build and enterprise-build columns are therefore not strictly comparable to each other. The final column, which excludes invoices auto-approved under the ₹25,000 rule, can only be computed from Q2 FY26 because the required event field was not emitted before 11 September 2025.
QuarterAs reportedMain buildEnterprise buildExcl. auto-approved
Q4 FY2544%42%not comparableno data
Q1 FY2658%55%not comparableno data
Q2 FY2666%63%not comparable51%
Q3 FY2671%69%not comparable52%

Source: recomputed by Kavya Srinivasan from the warehouse, 6–7 March 2026, not reviewed by anyone else.

Exhibit 2 contains the arithmetic that kept Kavya at the table. Read one way, the metric has risen 27 points and the product organisation has done excellent work. Read another way, the last two quarters of apparent gain — 66% to 71% — are accompanied by a recomputed figure that moved only one point, from 51% to 52%, which would imply that almost all of the recent improvement is the auto-approve rule rather than automation. Read a third way, the recomputed column is itself questionable: an invoice auto-approved under a rule the customer configured deliberately is being processed without human touch, and it is not obvious why that should not count.

Exhibit 4. Mid-market customers acquired in FY25, split by whether they reached the automation threshold within sixty days, followed for twelve months. Prepared by Tanya Oberoi, 6 March 2026. Segment mix is not controlled for; the note in her file reads "activation and invoice complexity are correlated and I have not separated them."
CohortAccountsMedian monthly invoices12-month churnNet expansion on survivorsACV (₹ lakh)
Reached threshold in 60 days31841021.7%+6%9.4
Did not reach in 60 days2661,9806.4%+24%21.8

Churn is contract non-renewal within twelve months of go-live. Expansion is change in contracted value on renewed accounts.

Exhibit 4 is the exhibit that inverts the case. On its face it says that the input metric the product organisation has been managing for a year is negatively associated with the outcome the board tracks. Read more carefully, it says something less dramatic and possibly more damaging: accounts that automate quickly are accounts with simple, low-volume invoice flows — a median of 410 invoices a month against 1,980 — and those are precisely the accounts for which Tally plus a clerk, or Zoho's bundled module, is a rational substitute. Activation-60 may be a good measure of nothing more than customer simplicity. Whether the causation runs from fast activation to churn, or from simplicity to both, the exhibit cannot say, and Tanya explicitly declines to say it.

Exhibit 5. The exception queue, Bengaluru operations, monthly. Lekha's contracts commit to resolving customer-raised invoice exceptions within one business day for mid-market and four hours for the enterprise edition. Headcount and cost are for the 19-person exceptions desk in Bengaluru.

January and February include the post-mandate filing peak. The 4-hour enterprise SLA is reported separately and stood at 96% and 93%; Grace Chan's informal concessions to Al Mirzam are not reflected in either series.

Exhibit 5 is the exhibit nobody had put next to the others. Exceptions are what remains after automation, and they are rising faster than volume: up 49% since September against invoice-volume growth of about 22%. Median resolution time has tripled. If the thing customers actually buy is that their exceptions get resolved, then the binding constraint on retention may sit in a nineteen-person desk in Bengaluru costing ₹25.9 lakh a month, and not in activation at all. Whether the exception rise is caused by the auto-approve rule pushing errors downstream, by the filing peak, or by the mix of newly onboarded accounts, the exhibit does not distinguish.

Exhibit 6. Vendor-portal weekly active suppliers per account, and subsequent renewal, main build only. Tanya Oberoi's December 2025 model. The series is discontinued from 15 January 2026 because supplier-level activity tracking was removed in the DPDP consent re-architecture; the last two rows are partial.
Quartile of weekly active suppliersAccountsRenewedRenewal rateData available after 15 Jan 2026
Top quartile22521495%No

Fitted on 900 accounts; 780 of them fall in the ₹6–12 lakh annual-contract band. Not validated out of sample. No equivalent instrumentation exists on the enterprise build.

Exhibit 6 was, until January, the most promising candidate to replace Activation-60: a 33-point renewal spread, readable weekly, and about a thing Lekha could influence through supplier onboarding campaigns. Two facts spoil it. The instrumentation no longer exists in the same form. And, as Tanya's unpublished caveat records, the model was fitted almost entirely within one contract band, so the spread may be measuring account size rather than account health.

7. Voices

Anirudh Varma to Kavya Srinivasan, WhatsApp, Saturday 7 March, 22:11 IST

"I hear you on the definition. But understand what you are asking. We restate page nine on Monday, the board asks when we knew, and I have to say Wednesday. Then the fund asks the same question. Is the 52 more true than the 71 or is it just more conservative? Because those are different things and only one of them is a reason to blow up a round."

Rajat Bhandari, engineering all-hands, Pune, 26 February 2026

"I want to be precise about this. We are not bad at measuring. We are measuring two products and calling them one. Everything downstream of that — the activation number, the retention cut, the exception SLA split — inherits the problem. You can argue about which metric goes on the slide. You cannot fix the slide."

Nikhil Iyengar, email to Anirudh Varma and Kavya Srinivasan, 7 March, 09:40 EST

"Please loop me in before anything changes. Four of my nine open opportunities reference the sixty-day claim in the deck we published in October. One of them has asked me, in writing, for the methodology. I can hold that for maybe three weeks. If the number changes I need to know what the new number is and whether it is auditable, not that the old one was wrong."

Grace Chan, customer-success weekly, Singapore, 3 March 2026

"Nobody at Al Mirzam has ever asked me about activation. They ask about the Thursday reconciliation and whether the Arabic capture is reading their Jebel Ali invoices. Forty-one accounts. I can tell you the health of each of them from memory and I do not need a dashboard to do it. What I need is four engineers who do not get moved in April."

Tanya Oberoi, message in the analytics channel, 6 March, 21:02 EST

"I want to flag that I am being asked to compare cohorts that differ in invoice complexity by a factor of five. I can produce a matched analysis but I need three weeks and a complexity feature that does not currently exist in the warehouse. Anything I give you before that is directional at best. Please do not put a decimal point on it."

Jonas Keller, design review, Berlin, 20 February 2026

"The threshold should go to fifty thousand. Nineteen customers asked for twenty-five and eleven have since asked for more. I understand there is a metrics question. From where I sit the metrics question is your problem and the customers are mine."

Meghna Rao, note attached to the board pack, 8 March, 17:30 IST

"For the record: I have asked since November for a single retention definition. The pack still contains mine and product's. I am content to present either. I am not content to present both without saying which one we manage to."

8. The options as Kavya currently sees them

First, restate. Put the recomputed series on page nine, explain the auto-approve interaction, drop the flagship figure from 71% to 52%, and accept the consequences with the board, the fund and Nikhil's pipeline. The virtue is that everything afterwards is built on something true. The costs are concrete: an unquantifiable effect on the term sheet, a methodology conversation with an Ohio procurement department, and a restated series whose earlier quarters — as Exhibit 3's dashed line concedes — cannot actually be recomputed, only reconstructed.

Second, keep and guard. Leave Activation-60 as reported, add two guardrails — touchless rate excluding auto-approved invoices, and median exception resolution time — and manage all three from April. This preserves continuity, gives the board a richer picture without a restatement, and is what most companies do. It also means the number on page nine remains one that Kavya has privately concluded is inflated, and the guardrails will be read as supporting detail rather than as the correction they are.

Third, split the operating model. Run the mid-market book on an input register and the forty-one enterprise accounts on named-account judgement, as Grace wants, and stop pretending a consolidated Activation-60 means anything. This is honest about the fork and cheap in the short run. It also formalises the 2022 decision Kavya and Anirudh have been trying to reverse for two years, and it hands Rajat an argument for never unifying the codebase.

Fourth, change what is measured entirely. Abandon activation as the product organisation's input and adopt exception-resolution performance instead, on the reading of Exhibit 5 that the queue is the binding constraint. This has the appeal of attacking something visibly deteriorating. It also rests on one uncontrolled exhibit, requires headcount Meghna has not budgeted, and would be the second flagship metric change in twelve months.

The framing has a feature Kavya noticed at around eleven and had not resolved by midnight: all four options are answers to the question "what should the product organisation's metric be", and Exhibit 4 may be asking a different question. If fast activation identifies accounts that were always going to leave because the product is over-specified for them, then the metric is not wrong; the segment is. Nobody in the company had proposed that Lekha should stop selling to the 318.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at 10:00 IST on Monday 9 March. The pack has been circulated. Nikhil, on New Jersey time, will be asleep for the first half of it; Tanya likewise. Grace joins from Singapore. The Singapore fund's term sheet, as Anirudh describes it, has an exclusivity window expiring 27 March.

The Al Mirzam contract runs to 30 June 2026 and carries a ninety-day renewal notice clause, which means notice is due by 31 March — three weeks after the board meeting and four days after the term sheet window closes. Grace's informal concessions are unrecorded and unpriced.

Engineering's FY27 budget is ₹18 crore. Rajat's estimate to unify the codebase and the event schema is eleven to fourteen months of roughly a third of the team, which he prices at ₹6.2 crore and which Meghna has provisionally allocated at ₹3 crore. Two senior engineers on the fork are a resignation risk by July; their replacement cost in the Bengaluru market, Rajat estimates, is 35% above their current bands.

The complexity feature Tanya needs to control Exhibit 4 properly does not exist and would take three weeks to build. The DPDP consent architecture cannot be reversed. The published case study containing the seventy-one per cent claim is a PDF on Lekha's site and in four active American deals.

10. Questions for discussion

1. Sort every number in Exhibits 1 to 6 into two groups: those a named team at Lekha could deliberately move within one quarter, and those the company can only report. Which group does page nine of the board deck belong to, and which group did Lekha believe it belonged to?

2. Exhibit 1 presents two net-revenue-retention series that differ by five points and have never been reconciled, while mid-market gross churn rises underneath both. What is each series good for, and what does the fact that both were circulated for fifteen months tell you about how Lekha's measurement system is governed?

3. Exhibit 2's final column and Exhibit 3's dashed segment are not the same kind of evidence. Which parts of Kavya's recomputation would survive a hostile reading by an auditor or an investor, and which would not? Does the distinction change what she is obliged to say on Monday?

4. Exhibit 4 shows the managed input negatively associated with the tracked outcome, with a five-fold difference in invoice complexity between the cohorts and no controls. Construct the two strongest incompatible interpretations of that exhibit, and state what evidence would separate them and how long it would take to obtain.

5. Grace Chan claims she can hold the health of forty-one accounts in her head and does not need a dashboard; Rajat Bhandari claims none of the measurement can be fixed while the fork exists. Both may be right. What would an operating model look like that accepted both claims, and what would it cost Lekha in the FY27 budget and in the July engineering-retention risk?

6. What should Kavya do on Monday morning, and in what order — what she puts on page nine, what she says about when she knew, what she asks the board to decide rather than to note, and what she commits to bring back and by when? If the board asks her directly whether the seventy-one per cent is true, what is her answer?

11. Midnight

At ten past twelve Kavya opened the deck and looked at page nine again. The chart was clean. The axis started at zero. The source line read "Lekha product analytics, February 2026", which was accurate.

She thought about the sentence she had used at the April offsite, which people had repeated approvingly for a year: give the teams something they can actually move, and let the board watch the outcome. It had been right. The teams had moved something. Whether they had moved the thing, or moved the measurement of the thing, or moved a number that identified customers Lekha should never have sold to, were three different failures with three different remedies, and she could not tell from her own data which one she was in.

Tanya's message sat unanswered. Anirudh's sat unanswered. Nikhil's email was marked as read. In nine hours and fifty minutes she would have to say something, and the only sentence she had written on the A4 sheet, at some point she could not remember, was a question rather than a statement: what would I have needed to know in August to have caught this?

She closed the laptop, and then opened it again.

Case · Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation · Product Metrics & Measurement

Sarathi Loads: The Flat Line on the Board Slide

Ahmedabad, February 2026. A trucking marketplace's headline number has stopped moving. The chief executive wants a growth push. The head of product wants to know which numbers anyone actually controls.

1. Monday morning, Prahlad Nagar

At twenty past eight on Monday, 2 February 2026, Nandini Joshi walked into Sarathi Loads' office in Prahlad Nagar, Ahmedabad, with a printout she had made at home because she did not trust herself to read it calmly on a screen in a meeting. It was a single line chart: loads matched per week, the number that appeared on slide three of every board deck Sarathi had produced since 2023. The line rose steeply for five quarters and then, from roughly the second week of October 2025, went flat. Nine thousand four hundred loads a week, give or take eighty, for fifteen consecutive weeks.

Nandini was vice-president of product. On the previous Friday, Sarathi's chief executive, Ronak Desai, had sent a two-line message to the leadership group: the March board meeting needed a growth plan, and he wanted a proposal by Friday, 6 February. His own view, stated in the same message, was that Sarathi should cut its commission from 3.8% of freight value to 2.9% for a quarter and put ₹6 crore behind shipper incentives. "We know the number we need to move," he had written. "Let us move it."

Nandini did not disagree that the number needed to move. What bothered her was that she could not find anybody in the company who could move it. Loads matched per week was a result. It was produced by four separate things happening in sequence across three teams, two of which sat in different time zones, and Sarathi's quarterly planning sheet contained none of those four things. It contained, instead, the result, restated four times in four teams' goals.

2. Company background

Sarathi Loads was founded in 2021 by Ronak Desai and Pritesh Shah, both formerly of a Surat textile exporter's logistics arm, on a simple observation about the Indian road-freight market: the large organised players — Delhivery, Mahindra Logistics, BlackBuck, Porter, Rivigo's successors — had modernised the segments with predictable volumes, while the fragmented long-haul market of single-truck and five-truck owners still ran on telephone calls to commission agents in transport nagars.

Sarathi built a load-matching marketplace. A shipper — typically an FMCG distributor, a Morbi ceramic-tile unit, a Tiruppur garment exporter or a third-party logistics firm serving Flipkart or Reliance Retail sellers — posted a load with origin, destination, tonnage, vehicle type and pickup window. Transporters bid. Sarathi took a commission on the accepted freight value, handled the e-way bill linkage required under GST, held FASTag-based tracking, and released payment to the transporter against a proof of delivery uploaded in the driver app. By January 2026 it had about 61,000 verified transporters, 2,900 active shippers and a run rate of roughly ₹1,370 crore of annualised freight value.

Two adjacent bets shaped the team. In 2024 Sarathi added a cross-border documentation module for exporters shipping through Mundra and Nhava Sheva, which brought in a Dubai-based building-materials importer, Al Mirzam Group, as its largest single account by freight value — ₹94 crore annualised, moving Morbi tiles to Jebel Ali. In 2025 it hired a sales head in New Jersey to sell a lane-visibility feed to American freight brokers, a small revenue line that nonetheless consumed a disproportionate share of engineering attention.

3. The situation

Sarathi's weekly leadership review ran on Tuesday mornings and consisted of six charts, all of them results. Exhibit 1 reproduces the central series.

Exhibit 1. Sarathi Loads, weekly averages by quarter. Freight value is the amount shippers pay transporters; commission revenue is Sarathi's take. Figures for Q4 FY26 cover the first five weeks only.

Q2 FY269,20025.83.8%98

Source: Sarathi internal marketplace ledger, extracted 31 January 2026.

What the review never showed was the sequence that produced the 9,400. Nandini asked Simran Kaur, the data scientist in Toronto, for it on 28 January, and received it two days later at 03:40 IST. Exhibit 2 is her funnel.

The funnel changed the conversation, or would have if the conversation had happened. Nearly four thousand loads a week — worth roughly ₹10.9 crore of freight value and about ₹41 lakh of foregone weekly commission — were being posted and left unbid. Four-fifths of them sat on thirty-eight lanes where Sarathi had thin transporter supply: Morbi to Guwahati, Coimbatore to Raipur, Ludhiana to Vijayawada, and thirty-five others of the same character, long hauls with no reliable return load.

Wei Lin Tan, the customer-success lead in Singapore, saw the same phenomenon from the account side and described it differently. Her monthly note of 20 January reported that eleven shippers had reduced posting volume in the December quarter, and that in nine of the eleven cases the stated reason was not price but unreliability: "they say they cannot plan a dispatch around a platform that sometimes finds a truck in ten minutes and sometimes not at all." Al Mirzam's procurement manager in Dubai had put it more bluntly on a call at 11:00 Gulf time, which was 12:30 in Ahmedabad and the middle of Lena Fischer's morning in Berlin: the group would keep its Mundra volumes on Sarathi only if the platform committed to a confirmed truck within two hours for its named lanes.

Simran's third exhibit, which Nandini had not asked for, was the one that unsettled her most.

Exhibit 3. Shippers acquired between April and September 2025, grouped by the on-time pickup performance of their first three loads. "Still posting" means at least four loads posted in January 2026.

Source: Simran Kaur, 30 January 2026. Footnote in the original: lanes are not controlled for; shippers on dense western-corridor lanes both get better pickups and post more for reasons unrelated to Sarathi's performance.

The spread was 48 percentage points. If the relationship held even at half strength, the first three pickups of a new shipper's life were worth more to Sarathi's growth than the commission rate was — and unlike the commission rate, pickup reliability was something Karthik Menon's dispatch team in Pune could work on directly.

4. The people

Ronak Desai, chief executive, Ahmedabad. He had raised a Series B of ₹240 crore in mid-2025 on a growth story and had a March board meeting in which a flat line would be read as the story ending. He wanted a plan whose effect would be visible before the meeting after that. He was not hostile to Nandini's funnel; he simply did not believe the company had two quarters to spend on it.

Karthik Menon, engineering lead, Pune, with 34 engineers split between Pune and Bengaluru. He had been asking for two quarters for permission to rebuild the bid-notification system, which currently pushed a single notification to transporters matching a lane and vehicle type and then went quiet. He believed, without evidence he could point to, that most of the 3,900 unbid loads were unbid because the right transporter never saw them.

Wei Lin Tan, customer success, Singapore. Her incentive was account retention, and her commercial reality was Al Mirzam. She favoured any option that let her promise a confirmed truck on named lanes, and she was privately opposed to a commission cut because her largest accounts negotiated on reliability and would simply bank the discount.

Simran Kaur, data scientist, Toronto. She had built the funnel and the cohort table and was careful to say in writing that neither established causation. She wanted a randomised test on the dispatch rule before anyone forecast anything from Exhibit 3, and she had noted that at Sarathi's volumes such a test would need about five weeks to read.

Pritesh Shah, co-founder and head of supply, Ahmedabad. He owned transporter onboarding and thought the thin-lane problem was a supply problem that money solved: put a price guarantee on the thirty-eight lanes and transporters would come.

5. The options

Option A — the commission push. Cut the take rate from 3.8% to 2.9% for one quarter and spend ₹6 crore on shipper posting incentives. The upside is speed and legibility: posting volume would almost certainly rise, the board metric would move, and the plan needs no new instrumentation. The cost is ₹6 crore of incentive plus roughly ₹4.2 crore of foregone commission over the quarter, and the structural objection is that the intervention targets the top of the funnel while the losses are in the middle. If 3,900 of 16,800 posted loads already go unbid, adding posted loads on thin lanes adds unbid loads.

Option B — the input register. Replace the four teams' restatements of "loads matched per week" with three owned input metrics: thirty-minute bid coverage on the thirty-eight thin lanes, owned by Pritesh; on-time pickup within window for the first three loads of every new shipper, owned by Karthik; and proof-of-delivery upload within six hours, owned by operations. Each gets a weekly review, a named owner and one randomised test in the quarter to establish its elasticity, with Simran's five-week read built into the schedule. The upside is that the company would, for the first time, be managing things it controls. The cost is that nothing conclusive can be shown to the March board, and the plan reads as process rather than growth.

Option C — the thin-lane guarantee. Attack one constraint only. On the thirty-eight thin lanes, Sarathi commits a confirmed truck within two hours at a published price, taking the spread risk onto its own books, with a ₹2.4 crore risk budget for the quarter. The upside is that it addresses the largest identified leak, satisfies Al Mirzam's demand and produces a visible promise Wei Lin can sell. The cost is balance-sheet exposure on exactly the lanes where Sarathi's price knowledge is weakest, and a service commitment that, if broken, damages the reliability reputation the option exists to build.

6. Questions for discussion

1. List the numbers Sarathi currently reviews weekly, and sort each into two buckets: those a named team can move within one quarter, and those the company can only report. What does the sorted list tell you about why four teams all had the same goal?

2. Exhibit 3 shows a 48-point retention spread by first-three-pickup performance, and its own footnote warns that lanes are not controlled for. How much of that spread would you be willing to act on, and what is the cheapest evidence that would let you act on more of it?

3. Ronak needs something to show a board in March; Simran needs five weeks to read a test. Is that conflict real, or is it a disagreement about which number is being shown? What could Nandini put in front of the board that is both honest and not merely a promise of process?

4. Which option should Nandini propose by Friday, and what exactly would she commit to measure, on what cadence, with whom accountable? If she is wrong, when would she know?

7. A note for the learner

The lens that organises this case is the separation between metrics you can act on and metrics you can only report. Loads matched per week is an output: it is the joint product of posting volume, bid coverage, match rate, pickup reliability and delivery confirmation, and no single team at Sarathi can move it on purpose. Ronak's instinct — move the number directly — is the characteristic error of an organisation whose dashboard contains only results. The commission rate is a lever, but it is a lever on the first step of a funnel whose losses are concentrated in the second and fourth.

A well-reasoned answer does three things. It distinguishes the two axes that the case quietly sets up: controllability (bid coverage and pickup performance are controllable by named teams; freight rates and competitors' promotional intensity are not) and latency (posting volume responds in days; shipper retention responds in months). It notices that Exhibit 3 is a cohort comparison and not an experiment, and that its own footnote names the confound. And it insists that every metric proposed for the plan arrive with an owner, a cadence and the decision it informs — the discipline that Sarathi's planning sheet lacks entirely.

One defensible path runs roughly as follows. Nandini proposes Option C as the visible commitment and Option B as the operating system underneath it, and declines Option A for this quarter. The reasoning: the thin-lane guarantee attacks the single largest measured leak in the funnel — about ₹41 lakh of weekly commission left on the table — and produces exactly one controllable input, thin-lane bid coverage, whose movement can be read within three weeks because Sarathi itself sets the guarantee. That gives Ronak a growth action with a number attached before the March board. Simultaneously she puts the first-three-pickup metric into a weekly review under Karthik with a randomised dispatch-priority test starting the first week of the quarter, so that by the following board meeting the company has a measured elasticity rather than Exhibit 3's correlation. She keeps loads matched per week as the reported output, owned by herself, explicitly not assigned to any team, and reconciled monthly against the inputs. Option A is held in reserve on the honest ground that a commission cut is the one intervention the company can execute at any time and cannot easily reverse.

The path is defensible, not uniquely correct. A reader who argues that Al Mirzam's two-hour demand makes Option C a dangerous promise on lanes where Sarathi's pricing is weakest, and who instead funds Option B alone with a candid board conversation about a quarter of instrumentation, is making a reasonable case. What is not defensible is a plan that sets four teams a target on a number none of them controls, which is what Sarathi had been doing for five quarters while the line still happened to be going up.

Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation · Product Metrics & Measurement

Input vs Output; Leading vs Lagging

Which metrics can I act on, and which do I only report?

1. A number that will not move

On the second Monday of August 2026, Aanya Kohli walked into Godam Basket's weekly leadership review in Pune carrying a slide she did not want to present. Godam Basket delivered groceries to 1.2 million weekly active users across nine cities, and the company's North Star metric — orders per active user per week, OAUW for short — had slipped from 2.4 to 2.3 over the previous quarter. That tenth of an order sounds small until you multiply it by 1.2 million users: it was roughly 120,000 fewer orders a week, and at an average order value of ₹380, close to ₹4.6 crore of weekly revenue that was not showing up.

The CEO's question was blunt: what is the product team doing about it? Aanya's team already tracked a wall of numbers — app opens, push notification click-through, search-to-cart clicks, cart abandonment, payment failures. Some of these had been written into the quarter's OKRs as things the team would "move." But when Aanya pressed her own engineers in the run-up to the review, she got uncomfortable answers. Nobody could point to a specific feature that would change OAUW directly. Several people could point to features that changed search-to-cart clicks. The team had been setting goals on a number it could report, and calling it a number it could act on. Getting that distinction right, and getting the team's OKRs onto the right side of it, was the actual decision in front of Aanya that Monday.

2. The idea, precisely

An output metric is the result you ultimately care about: revenue, retention, orders per user. It is the outcome of many things happening together — marketing, product, pricing, competitors, even the weather — so no single team can move it directly by shipping one thing. Because it reflects everything that has already happened, it usually also moves late; by the time it changes, the causes are weeks or months behind you. That is what "lagging" means: the metric trails the actions that produced it.

An input metric is a specific, narrow number that a particular team can change through work they can actually ship this sprint or this quarter — a conversion rate on one screen, a failure rate on one payment flow. Because it responds quickly to the team's own work, it tends to move before the output does, which is what "leading" means: it gives you an early read on where the output is headed.

The idea has two parents. The lagging/leading indicator language comes from business planning generally and was formalised for management use by Robert Kaplan and David Norton's Balanced Scorecard, published in the Harvard Business Review in 1992, which argued that companies managed only by lagging financial results were steering by the rear-view mirror. The input/output framing as applied to product teams and OKRs was popularised inside Silicon Valley growth organisations in the 2010s, and travelled into product management alongside John Doerr's OKR methodology, precisely because teams kept discovering that an OKR set on an output metric produced frustration, not action. The sentence Aanya could say in that Monday review without sounding glib: "If my team can't name the exact thing they'd ship to move this number, it's an output we report, not an input we own."

3. How the split is actually made

The mechanics are a short discipline, and most of the value is in the steps practitioners skip because they feel obvious.

Start from the output. Aanya's output was OAUW, the company's North Star. Break it into a metrics tree — the same breadth-by-depth-by-frequency decomposition used to find a North Star's components — until the branches end in numbers that live on one screen or one flow, not the whole product. Test each leaf with one question: can a named team change this number through a change they could ship in the current cycle? If yes, it is a candidate input. If the number only moves because a dozen other things move together — seasonality, brand awareness, competitor pricing — it stays an output, however far down the tree it sits.

The step people leave implicit is the timing check: does the candidate input actually move ahead of the output, and by roughly how long? A metric that is technically actionable but shows no lead time over the output is not doing useful work as an early warning; it is just another lagging number measured more often. Only after both tests pass — actionable by a named team, and leading in time — does Aanya's team assign the metric an owner, a review cadence, and, crucially, the decision it is meant to inform. An input metric without a decision attached to it is a vanity number with better manners.

4. Godam Basket's tree, with real arithmetic

Aanya's team decomposed OAUW multiplicatively: orders per user per week equals sessions per user per week, times the share of sessions that convert into an order.

The arithmetic: 5.0 sessions × (61% × 83% × 91%) = 5.0 × 0.4607 = 2.30 orders per user per week, matching the observed OAUW. The three multiplied terms are the payments and checkout pod's actual inputs. Suppose that pod ships a fix for a known cause of UPI payment failures — a retry against an alternate handle when the first attempt times out — and payment success rises from 91% to 96%, with search-to-cart and cart-to-checkout unchanged.

QuantityBeforeAfter fix
Sessions / user / week5.05.0
Search→Cart click rate61%61%
Cart→Checkout start rate83%83%
Payment success rate91%96%
Session→Order conversion46.1%48.6%
OAUW (output)2.302.43

A gain of 0.13 orders per user per week is 5.7%. Across 1.2 million weekly active users, that is roughly 156,000 extra orders a week, or, at ₹380 average order value, about ₹5.9 crore of incremental weekly GMV — from a payment-retry change the team could scope, build, and ship in a sprint. Nobody shipped "OAUW." Somebody shipped payment success, and OAUW moved because it is built out of that number.

5. Nuances a learner has to sit with

Input is not a synonym for vanity metric. App downloads move constantly and feel input-like, but they are downstream of marketing spend, not of anything the product team ships, and they barely correlate with orders. A number qualifies as an input only if a named team can move it and it is known to matter to the output — both conditions, not one.
Leading and actionable are two different tests, often confused as one. Search interest in "grocery delivery near me" leads OAUW by weeks, but Aanya's team cannot ship anything that changes how many people search that phrase. A metric can be an honest early warning without being an input anyone owns.
Actionability is relative to the team asking, not a property of the number itself. Cart-to-checkout rate is an input for the checkout pod. For the category merchandising team, the same number is just context they read, because nothing they ship touches the checkout screen. The label changes with who is holding the roadmap.
The time horizon changes what counts as movable. Over one sprint, brand trust is a fixed output nobody can touch. Over eighteen months of reliable delivery, it becomes something a team can deliberately build. Don't confuse "not actionable this quarter" with "never actionable."
An input metric turned into an OKR gets gamed, not just improved. This is Goodhart's law showing up on a dashboard: the moment "payment success rate" becomes a target with a bonus attached, someone will find a way to inflate it — silently retrying a charge three times, for instance — without improving the customer's actual experience.
The correlation between an input and its output needs re-testing, not a one-time proof. Search-to-cart click rate predicted OAUW well in 2025; a change in UPI transaction limits or a rival's pricing move can quietly break that relationship in 2026. Treat the link as a hypothesis under continuous review, not a fact established once.
Chasing an input without a paired guardrail is how good intentions cause harm. The UPI retry fix that lifted payment success to 96% is only safe if a separate guardrail metric — duplicate-charge complaints — stays flat. Input metrics tell a team what to push; guardrails tell it what not to break while pushing.
The split tells you who owns what and where to look; it does not tell you the fix is worth doing, or that it even causes the output to move. A decomposition shows that payment success is arithmetically part of OAUW. It does not prove that raising it by shipping a particular fix is what actually moved the number, rather than a coincident marketing campaign. That proof still requires an experiment.

6. How the same idea looks in different businesses

In a consumer app like Godam Basket, inputs sit on short, visible funnels — search, cart, checkout, payment — and the feedback loop between shipping a fix and seeing the input move is days, sometimes hours. At Kaveri Ledger, a B2B accounting product sold to small manufacturers, the output that matters is net revenue retention, and the candidate inputs — how deeply a customer uses reconciliation features, how fast their support tickets close, whether onboarding finished within the first month — move on a much longer clock, because the thing that finally shows up in the output is a renewal decision made once a year. A team at Kaveri Ledger can ship an onboarding improvement in a sprint and still wait two quarters before the output metric shows anything, which changes how much patience the review cadence needs to have.

A marketplace complicates the picture further because the output is jointly produced by two sides that no single team fully controls. At Haat Bazaar, a marketplace connecting kirana wholesalers to small retailers, GMV is the output, and the input tree splits into a supply-side branch (how many wholesalers list stock, how reliably they fulfil) and a demand-side branch (how well retailer search surfaces relevant items). Improving the demand-side input does nothing to GMV if supply-side fill rate is the actual constraint that week — so marketplace teams have to check which side is binding before they trust an input's lead time. Stage matters too: at an early-stage company, one team can often see and move most of the tree directly, and cadences can be weekly; at a large company with many pods each owning a thin slice of the same tree, coordinating those slices adds lag of its own, and cadences and metric governance necessarily become more formal.

7. Common mistakes

Setting a team OKR directly on the output. Symptom: the OKR reads "increase OAUW to 2.6," and the team's retro never references a specific shipped change. Underlying error: treating an aggregate outcome as if it were a lever. Cheapest diagnostic: ask what exact feature, shipped this quarter, would move this number — if no one can answer in one sentence, rewrite the OKR one layer down the tree.

Dashboards nobody uses to decide anything. Symptom: a wall of charts that never comes up in sprint planning. Underlying error: metrics chosen because they were easy to instrument, not because a specific team owns a decision tied to them. Diagnostic: check whether the metric's owner field names one team, or reads "everyone."

Assuming correlation instead of testing it. Symptom: the input metric climbs for two quarters while the output stays flat. Underlying error: the input was chosen from the tree's arithmetic without confirming the effect actually holds at current scale, or the lag is longer than anyone budgeted for. Diagnostic: pull the last three quarters of both series side by side before locking the next OKR on that input.

Hitting the input target by gaming it. Symptom: payment success rate hits 96% on the dashboard while customer complaints about duplicate charges rise in the same week. Underlying error: optimising the proxy in isolation, with no counter-metric watching for the cheat. Diagnostic: for every input OKR, name the guardrail metric that would catch the obvious way to fake it, before the sprint starts, not after.

8. What good looks like

Six months on, Godam Basket's metrics review has a different shape. OAUW is still on the leadership deck, but no team's OKR is written against it — it is reviewed monthly as a report of how the whole system is doing. Three pods carry input OKRs one layer down: payments owns UPI success rate, reviewed weekly, paired with a duplicate-charge guardrail; checkout owns cart-to-checkout start rate, reviewed weekly; growth owns push notification click-through as a leading, partly-actionable number, reviewed fortnightly with an explicit note that it only partly explains sessions. Every input metric on the board has a name, a cadence, and a one-line answer to "what would we ship to move this."

9. What Aanya decided, and what to read next

At the August review, Aanya reclassified OAUW as a reported output with no single team accountable for moving it directly, and proposed three input OKRs — payment success, search-to-cart click rate, cart-to-checkout start rate — each with a named pod, a weekly cadence, and the payment-success goal paired with a guardrail on duplicate-charge complaints. The CEO's question changed from "what will you do about OAUW" to "which of these three will you fix first," which is a question a team can actually answer.

From here, three ideas extend this one directly: guardrail metrics, which stop an input OKR from being gamed the way payment retries nearly were; the hierarchy of engagement, which ranks which inputs matter most rather than treating all of them as equally worth chasing; and proxies for long-term value, which face the harder problem of inputs that stand in for an output too far away to measure directly at all.

Sit with two questions. First: for the next metric someone asks your team to move, can you name the exact feature or fix that would change it before the review is due — and if you can't, are you actually improving your understanding of the business, or just improving your reporting of it? Second: when did you last re-check whether your favourite input metric still predicts the output it was chosen for, rather than simply trusting the tree you built the day you chose it?

Godam Basket, Kaveri Ledger and Haat Bazaar are fictional companies created for this teaching material.
exp40v2-met.input.output:
Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation · Product Metrics & Measurement

Input vs Output, Leading vs Lagging

What separates a number a team can steer from one it can only report, how the lead time between them is actually measured, and why the arithmetic of a metrics tree confers no licence to believe it.

1. Two rooms, one week apart

On 3 September 2026, Aparna Sundaram, vice-president of product at Vaidoorya Labs, sat in a Hyderabad conference room with a chart that had become an accusation. Vaidoorya ran 210 collection centres and about 46,000 home blood-sample collections a week across Telangana, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka. Its board metric was annual revenue per serviced household, ₹3,180; its operating cousin was the 180-day repeat-booking rate, the share of households that book again within six months. That rate had fallen from 36.1% to 33.8% over five quarters. Against 2.9 million serviced households, each point was worth roughly ₹9 crore a year.

Aparna's difficulty was not a shortage of numbers — her team watched turnaround, phlebotomist punctuality, report-download rate, doctor-referral share and NABL audit findings. It was that the quarterly plan committed the product organisation to moving the repeat-booking rate by 2 points, and nobody could say which shipped change would do it. Her data lead in Bengaluru, Rohit Barve, had put the question sharply: of the variance in that weekly rate, how much did anything the product team shipped explain? His first estimate was 11%. The rest was pricing, a competitor's diagnostic-package promotion, the seasonal dengue spike, and households who had a bad experience in March not coming back in September.

Six days later and 1,500 kilometres north, Imran Sheikh, chief product officer at Wakeel Legal Cloud in Gurugram, faced the mirror image. Wakeel sold AI-assisted contract review to 74 enterprise customers on ₹128 crore of recurring revenue across 9,400 seats, and net revenue retention had fallen from 119% to 104% in a year. NRR is measured once a renewal cycle; by the time it moves, the decisions behind it are eleven months old. Imran had two candidate early indicators: the share of a customer's contracts routed through Wakeel rather than emailed around (28%), and the share of reviewer sessions in which at least one AI-suggested redline was accepted without edit (41%). Meenal Kulkarni, his machine-learning lead in Pune, believed the second was the driver; Thomas Zachariah, who ran customer success from Kochi, believed it was the first. Both had charts, neither had evidence that would settle it, and the planning lock was eighteen days away.

2. The idea, and the quarrel inside it

Strip the vocabulary back to two independent axes, because most confusion here comes from collapsing them into one. The first is controllability: what share of a metric's movement can a named team cause through work it can ship inside its own planning horizon? The second is lead time: does the metric move before, with, or after the outcome the business cares about? An input metric is high on the first axis, a leading indicator on the second. They correlate, which is why people conflate them, but the off-diagonal cells are populated: a competitor's price cut leads Vaidoorya's repeat rate by weeks and is entirely uncontrollable; Wakeel's report-generation latency is exquisitely controllable and, past a threshold, predicts nothing.

The lagging/leading language comes from business-cycle econometrics: Wesley Mitchell and Arthur Burns at the National Bureau of Economic Research sorted series into leading, coincident and lagging groups in 1938, on the explicit understanding that a leading series is a regularity estimated from history, not a lever — nobody proposed ending a recession by ordering firms to place machine-tool orders. The input/output framing came from operations, and then from Amazon's practice of separating controllable input metrics from output metrics in its weekly business review, as Colin Bryar and Bill Carr describe in Working Backwards. The problem it solves is specific: teams given an output goal either do nothing legible or do everything at once, while teams given a controllable input goal ship. The cost is equally specific — a team can hit an input target with perfect fidelity and produce no business at all.

Four schools disagree, and what each will and will not sign is worth stating. The controllable-input school signs that every team goal should be a metric the team can move by its own shipping, and that green inputs against a flat output mean the inputs were chosen wrongly; it will not sign that inputs need experimental proof before adoption, since iteration on selection is the proof. The metrics-tree school signs that outputs decompose arithmetically and the leaves are the natural inputs: an identity plus a clear owner is enough to organise work. The causal-inference school signs the opposite: no metric is leading until the lead is measured and the link tested, and an identity is a tautology that cannot be falsified. The systems school, after Deming, signs that inputs are instruments of learning and should never carry targets, because a target on a component optimises the component and degrades the system.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Expert practice adds four steps usually left implicit: estimate controllability, measure the lead, size the leverage, set cadence from the measurement.

Step one: estimate controllability instead of asserting it

Rohit Barve differenced 78 weeks of each candidate metric and regressed the weekly change on indicators for the team's own releases, promotions, competitor promotions and epidemiological season. The variance attributable to releases is a blunt but honest controllability estimate: turnaround compliance 61%, report-download 44%, doctor-referral share 8%, the repeat-booking rate itself 11%. This is the number that should decide what goes on an OKR, and almost nobody computes it.

Step two: measure the lead, on differences, not levels

The tempting test is to plot indicator and outcome together and admire the fit. On raw levels, Vaidoorya's two series correlated at r = 0.81 at every lag from zero to eight weeks — the signature of two trending series, carrying no timing information. On differences the picture separates.

Turnaround compliance against the 180-day repeat-booking rate, Vaidoorya Labs, 78 weeks to August 2026. Levels are contaminated by common trend; differences locate the lead at three weeks.
Lag (weeks)0123456
r, raw levels0.810.810.800.810.800.790.79
r, first differences0.090.210.380.520.440.260.12

Three weeks is roughly how long a household with a pending prescription takes to book the follow-up test, and that number governs what follows. Sample an indicator twice inside its lead time to catch a turn early, so three weeks demands a weekly review and makes a monthly one useless. It sets the attribution window for experiments, and says how long to wait before calling a change a failure: a team that abandons a fix after two flat weeks abandoned it before the signal could arrive.

Step three: size the leverage, not the correlation

Correlation ranks indicators by how well they predict. Planning needs them ranked by how much outcome an engineering week buys: elasticity, times remaining headroom given where the input already sits, divided by cost. That reversed Vaidoorya's ranking.

Leverage per engineering week, September 2026. Elasticity is points of repeat-booking rate per 10 points of input movement; headroom is what the team judged achievable in two quarters.
Candidate inputNowElasticityHeadroomEng-wksOutput pts / eng-wk
Turnaround under 12 hrs78%2.7+9 pts260.093
Report-download rate71%1.4+14 pts90.218
Slot confirmed in 2 hrs92%3.1+4 pts180.069
Doctor-referral share23%4.0+6 pts400.060

Turnaround has the reputation and the second-highest elasticity. Report-download rate — whether the household opens the result in the app rather than taking a PDF on WhatsApp — has an unglamorous 1.4 and the cheapest path to a large move: a notification sequence and a one-tap login, nine engineering weeks. On leverage it beats turnaround two to one. Slot confirmation has the highest elasticity and is useless as a target, because at 92% there is nothing left to win. Elasticity without headroom is the commonest error here.

Step four: know your noise floor before you react

At a weekly denominator of 18,000 households and p = 0.34, one week's rate carries a standard error of 0.35 points and a week-on-week difference about 0.50, so the 95% band on movement is roughly ±1.0 point. Smaller wobbles are noise the review had been spending twenty minutes explaining. Drawing that band on the dashboard removed more bad decisions than any redefinition.

The second-order effects

Three effects separate naive application from competent. Saturation: elasticity is local. The 2.7 for turnaround came from a range of 71% to 80%; pushing to 95% will not return proportionately, since the households whose behaviour turns on turnaround are exhausted first. Composition: improving an input changes the mix passing through it — when Wakeel raised routing share, the newly routed contracts were low-stakes ones nobody had bothered to upload, mechanically lowering value per reviewed contract. Reflexivity: the relationship was estimated where nobody was optimising the indicator; once it is a target, the cheapest ways to move it are not the historical ways, so the elasticity decays. This is the Lucas critique in a product-management hat, and why leads and elasticities need re-estimating every few quarters.

4. When the idea applies, as testable claims

One: the team's own shipping explains a material share of the input's variance — say above a third. Vaidoorya passes on turnaround (61%) and report-download (44%) and fails on doctor-referral share (8%), a medical-affairs metric in product clothing. Wakeel fails on both candidates: routing share moves on a general counsel's mandate, not on anything Imran ships, which is why Thomas in Kochi owns it.

Two: the lead is measurable and longer than the review cadence. Vaidoorya passes at three weeks against a weekly review. Wakeel's NRR is annual and its indicators monthly — a comfortable lead with a brutal consequence, since the loop is too slow for within-quarter learning.

Three: the output is genuinely composed of the inputs, not merely correlated with them. Vaidoorya's tree is compositional. Wakeel's is not: NRR is a procurement committee's decision, and no identity connects it to redline acceptance.

Four: the elasticity is stable enough to plan on. This fails most often and most quietly, and when it fails the idea becomes actively misleading: under a demand shock, where the historical relationship comes from another world; in businesses small enough that one account swamps the aggregate; and where the output is dominated by a factor outside the tree. Vaidoorya's repeat rate from March to May turns more on seasonal illness than on anything the dashboard holds, and a team told to move it through that window will be judged by the weather.

5. Hard edges

Multi-product. Wakeel sells contract review and a clause library, but NRR is measured per account, so both teams' inputs land on one output and neither can be credited. Mature firms use per-module attribution everyone knows is approximate, and say so rather than litigating it quarterly.

Two-sided. At Vithika Bazaar, a Surat marketplace connecting fabric wholesalers to tailoring units, fill rate is an input for the supply team and an output for the demand team — one number, two labels, depending on who is looking. This is the general case: every input is someone else's output. The failure is the metric sitting on the boundary, where each side treats it as the other's input and nobody ships against it.

Regulated. Vaidoorya cannot treat tests per household as an input; ordering pathology tests is a clinical decision, and NABL accreditation and ICMR guidance limit what a diagnostics company may nudge. The expert response is to carve the tree into a clinically neutral region where inputs may be optimised and a clinically loaded region where metrics are reported and never targeted — in writing, before anyone is tempted.

Hardware plus software. Wardhan Instruments, which makes connected cold-chain sensors for dairy and vaccine logistics, has 41,000 units in the field, ships firmware quarterly, and updates out of cycle only devices that come in for service. If 6% of the base is serviceable per quarter, an input requiring firmware has a movable population of 2,460 units and can travel at most 6% of its range. Hardware changes the denominator, not the concept, and teams that ignore this diagnose a failed fix when they have measured a diluted one.

AI-native. Wakeel's deepest problem is non-stationarity: when Meenal swaps the model, every input baseline moves at once, breaking the elasticities the plan depends on. The handling is a frozen evaluation set re-scored on each model change, so a shift splits into "the world changed" and "we changed the model". Mature teams also accept that their most important input — whether a reviewer trusts the output — is badly measured by acceptance rate, since a lawyer who accepts everything may be trusting or exhausted.

6. What separates an expert

An identity is not evidence. A decomposition that multiplies exactly to the output is true by construction and unfalsifiable: it says where a number sits, not that moving it moves anything. The tell is a beautifully balanced tree whose owners have never experimented on a branch. The identity would hold equally if causality ran backwards.
Controllability is a fraction, not a flag. Competent practitioners sort metrics into actionable and not; experts quote the share of variance their own shipping explains and behave differently at 60% than at 15%. The tell is a PM who answers "how much of last quarter was us?" with a figure and a method rather than a story.
Lead time belongs to a pair, and it drifts. Turnaround leads repeat bookings by three weeks for Vaidoorya's chronic-care households and nine for annual-checkup ones; the aggregate describes neither. The tell is a team that re-measured within two quarters and found the lead had moved. Treating lead time as fixed is how cadences end up set by habit.
Elasticity without headroom is theatre. The highest-elasticity metric is usually the most optimised already, because it was obvious to everyone before you. Experts multiply by remaining room and divide by cost before ranking. The tell is a roadmap that declines the best coefficient and explains why in one sentence.
Surrogation is the real risk, not gaming. Gaming is conscious and detectable; surrogation — unconsciously substituting the measure for the thing it stands for — is invisible from inside the team. The tell is a team that argues the output must be miscalculated whenever its inputs are green. That argument is occasionally correct, which is what makes it dangerous.
The best input often lives outside the product. Vaidoorya's second-strongest predictor of repeat booking was whether the same phlebotomist visited a household twice — a rostering variable owned by operations in Vijayawada, with no product surface. Experts hand such a metric to the team that can move it, then read that team's numbers aloud in their own review.
A rising input can shift the mix and flatten the output. If every segment improves and the aggregate does not, composition has changed — Simpson's paradox in operational dress. The tell is an expert who asks for the segment mix before asking for the tracking to be re-checked; the instinct that instrumentation is broken is usually wrong.
Some outputs have no usable inputs, and saying so is the skilled move. Brand trust after a data incident, or a customer whose new CFO has a cost mandate, will not yield to a metrics tree inside the planning horizon. Experts switch to named bets and guardrails instead of inventing a fake input. The tell is a plan that leaves an objective deliberately unmetricated, and says why.

7. How it changes by product type and stage

In consumer products the inputs sit on short funnels with days of feedback, and the binding constraint is statistical power at the segment level, not identification. In B2B and enterprise the constraint inverts: the output is a renewal decided annually by people who may never touch the product, so the link cannot be established from within-quarter data and must come from account-level panels, with all the confounding that implies. Platforms and marketplaces add the seam, where one side's input is the other's output and the binding side changes week to week. Hardware changes the denominator and adds a second clock: a firmware-dependent metric cannot move faster than the release train, however controllable it looks. AI products add non-stationarity, and their most decision-relevant input is usually a quality judgement manufactured through evaluation sets rather than read from logs.

Where the difference is not real it is worth saying plainly: the four steps are identical in all five settings, and only the parameters change. Stage matters more than sector. A seed-stage company with 900 users cannot estimate an elasticity usefully and should choose inputs by mechanism and judgement. A growth-stage company has the volume for real estimates and lacks the discipline to use them. A large company has both and loses to the seam instead, where every candidate input has three claimants or none.

8. Three worked examples

Vipanchi Learning: the input that held

Vipanchi Learning, a Pune competitive-exam tutoring app, took 90-day paid retention (44%) as its output and, as its input, the share of new subscribers attending a live class within 72 hours of purchase (38%). The differenced panel gave an elasticity of 0.62 points of retention per point of attendance and a lead of five weeks. Scheduling nudges and a guaranteed first slot lifted attendance to 51%: 13 × 0.62 = 8.1 predicted points. Actual movement over two quarters was 6.4 points, to 50.4%, the shortfall tracing to saturation exactly as theory says — the last four points came from students who would have attended anyway.

Wakeel Legal Cloud: manufacturing evidence when randomisation is impossible

Imran could not randomise routing share, which a customer's internal policy sets. He could randomise an offer. Wakeel ran an encouragement design across 60 eligible accounts: 30 received free migration assistance, 30 did not, and take-up among the treated was 34%. Twelve months on, the treated group's NRR ran 1.9 points above control — the intention-to-treat effect. Dividing by compliance gives the effect on accounts that actually moved: 1.9 / 0.34 = 5.6 points. The observational panel had predicted 6.5 points per 10 points of routing share. The experiment did not overturn the direction; it shrank the magnitude, and turned a correlation two halves of the company were arguing about into a number both would accept.

Varenya Fresh: the input that worked exactly as instructed

Varenya Fresh, a Chennai direct-to-consumer spice and cold-pressed-oil brand, set its output as 12-month revenue per customer, ₹4,260, and its input as the 30-day reorder rate, then 22%. The growth team was given a target of 30% and hit 31% in two quarters, largely through an escalating discount ladder triggered at day 18. The input went green. The output fell.
