9. Failure modes and their diagnostics

Target on an uncontrollable output. Early sign: the retrospective describes market conditions rather than shipped work. Diagnostic: what share of last quarter's movement was us? Cost if caught late: a planning cycle spent on work chosen for its narrative fit.

Lead time assumed, never measured. Early sign: the cadence is monthly because reviews have always been monthly. Diagnostic: how many weeks between the input turning and the output turning, and how do we know? Cost: good changes killed before their effect arrives, bad ones funded past the point of evidence.

Correlation adopted as causation. Early sign: the input climbs two quarters and the output does not. Diagnostic: what experiment, encouragement design or natural discontinuity supports this link? Cost: a roadmap aimed at a symptom.

Definitional drift. Early sign: a metric jumps the week an instrumentation change shipped. Diagnostic: has the definition, filter or denominator changed since the elasticity was estimated? Cost: forecasts that miss by amounts nobody can explain.

Surrogation. Early sign: the team disputes the output's calculation whenever inputs look good. Diagnostic: if this input rose 20% and the output fell, what would we conclude? A team that cannot answer has already substituted. Cost: quarters of confident, well-executed, valueless work — Varenya's case exactly.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Should inputs carry numeric targets? The controllable-input position rests on organisational rather than statistical evidence: firms that set goals on controllable inputs ship more and argue less, and the process self-corrects because inputs that fail to move outputs get visibly replaced. It would be wrong if surrogation is common enough that the Varenya failure costs more than the shipping cadence is worth. The systems position holds that this cost is underestimated, because failures get blamed on the wrong input rather than on the practice of targeting inputs at all; it would be wrong if teams without numeric targets simply drift, which is what most managers observe.

How much causal evidence is enough? The causal school argues that an unexperimented input is a hypothesis with a budget attached, and points to how often randomised tests shrink observational estimates — Wakeel's 6.5 becoming 5.6 is mild, and halvings are routine. It would be wrong if waiting costs more than acting on a biased estimate, which is plausible for cheap, reversible changes; the pragmatist reply is that most product decisions are exactly that, so reserving rigour for the few that are not is efficient allocation of a scarce capability.

Do metrics trees help or hurt? Proponents call a shared decomposition the cheapest coordination device a large organisation has. Critics say its arithmetic completeness manufactures false confidence, because a tree that adds up feels verified. Both describe real experience at companies of different sizes, and nobody has run the counterfactual. Two questions stay open: how many inputs a team should carry, where three to five is folklore; and how to re-base elasticities when an AI model swap shifts every baseline at once.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this argues about denominators and windows in the first ten minutes rather than the last; asks what share of the movement was us before asking what the movement was; treats every elasticity as an estimate with a vintage; sets cadence from a measured lead; will tell a chief executive that an objective has no usable input and must be managed by judgement; and, when inputs are green and the output flat, reaches first for the segment mix. The signature is unglamorous: fewer metrics, discussed longer, revised more often.

12. Two decisions

Aparna took the repeat-booking rate off her teams' objectives and made it a monthly reported output with no single owner. Two pods took weekly input objectives: report-download rate, on the leverage calculation, paired with a guardrail on unsolicited-notification complaints; and turnaround compliance, with an elasticity to be re-estimated in January. Doctor-referral share went to medical affairs, where the 8% figure said it belonged. Her closing line to the board was that the company had been measuring its results faithfully and its causes not at all.

Imran declined to choose between Meenal's candidate and Thomas's. He funded the encouragement design, accepted a twelve-month wait for the verdict, and meanwhile gave the product team a manufactured within-quarter surrogate — time from contract upload to first accepted redline — chosen because it was controllable and fast, with an explicit note that its link to NRR was unproven and would be tested. Whether it is defensible to run a quarter on an input you have labelled unproven is what his board asked, and it is not obvious.

Discussion questions. (1) Aparna's controllability estimates came from an observational regression on her own team's release calendar. What would make the 61% badly wrong, and how would you check cheaply? (2) Wakeel's experiment measured the effect on accounts that complied. When does that generalise to accounts that never would, and does Imran's plan depend on it? (3) Varenya met its input target and destroyed margin: was the error the definition, the target, or the missing guardrail — and which would you fix first in a company that will not give up numeric targets?

13. Going deeper

Breadth × depth × frequency generates the candidate inputs in the first place. Guardrail metrics answer Varenya's failure directly and belong alongside every input target, not after one goes wrong. Hierarchy of engagement ranks inputs by depth of commitment rather than ease of measurement, the ordering that survives saturation. Proxies for long-term value take up Wakeel's harder case, where the output is too distant to measure inside any planning cycle. What makes a good metric and vanity vs actionable metrics supply the selection criteria this page assumes; direct vs proxy, magnitude vs ratio is the vocabulary that would have caught Varenya's count-versus-quality error before the discount ladder shipped; and the GAME framework with acquisition, retention, monetisation actions connects input choice to the lifecycle stage attacked. The North Star metric is the output this whole apparatus exists to explain, which is why it should never be anyone's objective on its own.

Vaidoorya Labs, Wakeel Legal Cloud, Vithika Bazaar, Wardhan Instruments, Vipanchi Learning and Varenya Fresh are fictional companies created for this teaching material. Regulators and standards named are real and appear only as market context.
